candidates.statement: Although breaking symmetries is still very popular for mixed-integer linear programming, a few recent works, such as the work on Orbital Shrinking [@Fischetti2012; @Salvagnin2013; @Fischetti2017], challenge the idea that symmetry handling methods for mixed-integer linear programming must necessarily break symmetry.
For a careful comparison between Orbital Shrinking and the core point method, we recommend [@Fischetti2017 section 3].

A partition $(\MP,\MQ)$ of the rows and columns of $A$ is said to be *equitable* if for all $P\in \MP,Q\in\MQ$ it holds that $$\begin{aligned} \label{eq_folding_row_sums} \sum_{w\in Q} A_{v,w} &= \sum_{w\in Q} A_{v',w}\text{ for all } v,v'\in P\\ \label{eq_folding_col_sums} \sum_{v\in P} A_{v,w} &= \sum_{v\in P} A_{v,w'}\text{ for all } w,w'\in Q. \end{aligned}$$ In words, for every block of $A$ defined by $P,Q$, the row sums and columns sums restricted to elements in the block must be equal.

First, note that since $\MQ$ is an equitable partition of $\ell$ and $u$, that for any $Q\in \MQ$ we have $\ell'_Q = |Q| \ell_w$ for all $w\in Q$ and $u'_Q = |Q| u_w$, since the $l_w$ and $u_w$ entries must be identical for all $w\in Q$ and are summed by definition of $\transpose{\Pi_\MQ}$.

candidates.statement: As far as we are aware, the only other work that treats reflection symmetries computationally for MILP solvers is by Christophel, Güzelsoy and Pólik [@Christophel2014] and explores how reflection symmetries may be used in primal heuristics.
Later on, we will clarify how one should choose $\delta_w$ in such cases.

The notion of bipolar and unipolar parts in [\[def_symmetric\]](#def_symmetric){reference-type="ref" reference="def_symmetric"} is very similar to an observation by Bödi, Herr and Joswig [@Bodi2013], who show that the orbits of reflection symmetry groups are either unipolar or bipolar, where bipolar orbits must consist of only pairs $w^+,w^-$ for some subset of $W$.

Thus, bipolar parts must always contain pairs of variables and [\[def_symmetric\]](#def_symmetric){reference-type="ref" reference="def_symmetric"}[\[def_symmetric_col_bipolar\]](#def_symmetric_col_bipolar){reference-type="ref" reference="def_symmetric_col_bipolar"} follows.

By equitability of $\widehat{\MQ}$, we must have for all $w_1^\lambda,w_2^\lambda \in Q^\lambda$ that $\widehat{c}_{w_1^\lambda} = \widehat{c}_{w_2^\lambda}$ and $\widehat{u}_{w_1^\lambda} = \widehat{u}_{w_2^\lambda}$ hold.
Thus $Q^{-\lambda}\subseteq Q'$ must hold for some $Q'\in \widehat{\MQ}$.

Since $\MP_i'$ satisfies [\[def_symmetric\]](#def_symmetric){reference-type="ref" reference="def_symmetric"}[\[def_symmetric_row_bipolar\]](#def_symmetric_row_bipolar){reference-type="ref" reference="def_symmetric_row_bipolar"} by assumption, all elements of $P^{-\gamma}$ are also contained in $P'$, and must be partitioned according to their sums.
For any feasible linear program $\ell \leq u$ must hold, and it is then possible to choose $\delta \in \R^W$ such that $\ell \leq \delta \leq u$ holds.

If $\ell_w = -\infty$ and $u_w = \infty$ hold, then the choice of $\delta_w$ does not affect the transformed variable bounds and bipolarity may be detected in any case.\ Second, recall that we assumed that the symmetric equitable partitions must be bound-respecting.

The partition $(\widehat{\MP},\widehat{\MQ})$ of the split reformulation must satisfy for all $Q\in \widehat{\MQ}$ and any $w_1^s,w_2^s\in Q$ that $\ell_{w_1} - \delta_{w_1} = \ell_{w_2} - \delta_{w_2}$ and $u_{w_1} - \delta_{w_1} = u_{w_2}- \delta_{w_2}$ hold if $s_1 = s_2$ holds, and if $s_1 \neq s_2$ holds that $\ell_{w_1} - \delta_{w_1} = -u_{w_2} + \delta_{w_2}$ and $u_{w_1} - \delta_{w_1} = - \ell_{w_2} + \delta_{w_2}$ hold.
First, if a bipolar part contains row or columns sums with identical but nonzero values, then it must be converted to a unipolar part and added to the search stack.
Thus, this implies that $x_w$ and $\delta_w$ must be integral by the given conditions.

candidates.statement: More generally, we believe it would be interesting to understand in further detail how one should apply linear and affine transformations to linear programs in order to detect arbitrary symmetries.

More generally, one could investigate if knowledge of symmetries of a linear program can be used directly to improve the performance of the simplex algorithm without modifying the analyzed (symmetric) polytope.\ In [\[sec_dimred_milp\]](#sec_dimred_milp){reference-type="ref" reference="sec_dimred_milp"}, we extended DRCR to mixed-integer linear programs and highlight that affine TU decompositions may be used to aggregate integer variables.

However, this complicates the algorithm and requires a way to decide how equitable parts must refined in case they can not be augmented to the network matrix.\ Our detection algorithm may benefit from detecting and exploiting additional substructures.
Although this is not a bottleneck of our approach, a crossover procedure that uses the solution as an initial feasible point should be more efficient.
